title: Permanent vs Seasonal Christmas Lights: Which Is Right for Your Home?
metaTitle: Permanent vs Seasonal Christmas Lights Compared
metaDescription: Compare permanent 12V roofline lighting to seasonal Christmas lights and consumer strips on cost, install effort, safety, longevity and year-round use.
excerpt: Seasonal strings, adhesive strip lights and permanent roofline systems all light up a house, but they cost, install and hold up differently. Here is how the three actually compare for a Canadian home.
heroAlt: Side-by-side comparison of traditional seasonal Christmas light strings and a permanent black aluminum LED track under a roofline
keyTakeaways: Seasonal lights and consumer adhesive strips cost less upfront but are put up and taken down every year and typically last two to five seasons before failing.
A permanent 12V system costs more at installation but is used year round for holidays, sports, birthdays and everyday warm white, not just December.
Professional seasonal installs in Canada run roughly the same or more per season as the one-time cost of a permanent kit spread over a few years of ladder work saved.

body.text: Every homeowner lighting up a roofline is really choosing between three different products that all end up looking similar in a photo: traditional seasonal Christmas light strings, adhesive consumer LED strips, and a permanent 12V track system. They differ enormously in what they cost over time, how much work they take, how long they last, and what you can actually do with them the other eleven months of the year. None of the three is wrong for every home; the right answer depends on how you actually plan to use the lights.
The three options, briefly

Seasonal Christmas lights are the incandescent or LED string lights most Canadian homes have used for decades, hung on clips or hooks each November and taken down in January. Adhesive consumer strips, brands like Govee and Eufy are the most common, are a newer category: flexible LED strips that stick to fascia or gutters with an adhesive backing, usually app-controlled and often marketed for both holidays and everyday accent lighting. Permanent systems, the kits sold at Permanent Lighting Direct, are aluminum track permanently screwed to the fascia or soffit, holding sealed RGBW pucks wired together and run from a fixed 12V power supply and WiFi controller.
Upfront cost

Seasonal string lights are the cheapest entry point, often a few hundred dollars in string sets for an average home, though the number climbs quickly for larger properties or premium LED strings. Consumer adhesive strips typically run two to four dollars per foot, putting a 100 ft roofline in the $200 to $400 range for the strip itself, before mounting hardware or a power supply upgrade for longer runs. A permanent 12V kit costs more upfront: our 100 ft kit is $1,729.20, scaling from $1,265 at 50 ft up to $3,157 at 250 ft, all in Canadian dollars, kit only, for a DIY install. That is a real gap on day one.
Cost over several years

The comparison changes once you add up what seasonal lighting actually costs across multiple years. A professional seasonal install and removal in Canada typically runs $25 to $40 per foot per season, since it is skilled ladder labour performed twice a year, once to hang and once to take down. On a 100 ft roofline, that is $2,500 to $4,000 a year, every year, which exceeds the entire cost of a permanent 100 ft kit inside a single season. Even a DIY seasonal approach carries a hidden cost in strings that fade, break or get tangled and need replacing every two to five seasons, plus the recurring weekend labour of putting them up and taking them down twice a year, every year, indefinitely.

items: Seasonal strings (DIY): low upfront cost, but recurring replacement every few seasons plus your own labour twice a year, forever.
Seasonal strings (professional install): highest ongoing cost, $25 to $40 per foot per season, with nothing to show for it in the off-season.
Consumer adhesive strips: moderate upfront cost, shorter expected lifespan due to adhesive failure and UV exposure, visible wiring.
Permanent 12V kit: highest one-time cost, no recurring install labour or seasonal replacement, used year round rather than one month a year.

body.text: Installation effort and who can do it

Seasonal strings go up with clips and come down the same way, which is straightforward but repetitive, and it is ladder work done twice a year rather than once. Consumer adhesive strips stick on with peel-and-stick backing, which sounds easier but the adhesive is the weak point: it fails faster in direct sun and through freeze-thaw cycles than most buyers expect, and the wiring typically stays visible along the fascia rather than sitting inside a housing. A permanent kit takes more effort at install time, mounting aluminum track section by section with screws, running the power supply and controller, and planning power injection on longer runs, but it is a one-time job. Our installation guide at /how-it-works walks through the full process for anyone doing it themselves.
Durability and how long each option actually lasts

This is where the categories separate the most. Seasonal incandescent and basic LED strings are not built for permanent outdoor exposure and typically show failed sections, faded colour or broken bulbs within a few seasons, especially if stored poorly between uses. Consumer adhesive strips are rated for outdoor use but the adhesive bond and the strip's flexible substrate degrade under UV and freeze-thaw faster than a sealed, screwed-down system, and replacement is common inside three to five years. Permanent kit pucks are rated for 50,000 hours of use, tested to function down to minus 40 Celsius, sealed to an IP68 rating, and back by a 5-year parts warranty. At a few hours of use per night even with year-round use, 50,000 hours works out to multiple decades of service.
Appearance, control and everyday use

A permanent system is visually cleaner because the track is colour-matched to your fascia, black, white, wicker or brown, and mounted flush rather than clipped on with visible hooks and cords. It is also functionally different: a WLED-based WiFi controller (see our /wled-controller-setup-guide-for-permanent-lights for the full setup) gives 16 million colours, a warm white channel, scheduling and app control, which turns the system into something you use every night of the year, not just in December. Seasonal strings and most consumer strips offer simpler or no app control, and neither is designed to be left up permanently, so neither gets used outside the holiday window even when the hardware technically could handle it.

The single biggest practical difference is usage frequency. A permanent system gets used for Halloween orange, Canada Day red and white, birthday colours, sports team colours, and a plain warm white porch light the rest of the year, in addition to Christmas. A box of seasonal strings in the garage gets used in December and sits idle the other eleven months.
Safety considerations

Seasonal ladder work twice a year is one of the more common sources of fall injuries tied to holiday lighting, and it repeats annually for as long as you keep doing your own strings. A permanent system means one ladder session at install rather than two sessions every year indefinitely. Electrically, permanent kits run on 12V, plug into an existing outdoor GFCI outlet, and are CSA Class 2 low voltage, so a standard residential install needs no electrician or permit, similar in that respect to plugging in seasonal LED strings, but without the annual re-installation risk.
Resale, curb appeal and energy use
Resale value and curb appeal

A permanent lighting system is a visible, semi-permanent exterior upgrade, similar in category to updated eavestrough or a repainted front door, and homeowners planning to sell within a few years sometimes weigh this into the decision. A neatly colour-matched track that has been up for a season or two generally reads as a normal part of the roofline rather than a decoration, especially once set to a plain warm white for most of the year, and buyers touring a home in the evening notice clean, functional exterior lighting. Seasonal lights, by contrast, leave no trace once taken down, which matters if you are selling shortly after the holidays and do not want an installed system factored into a listing conversation either way.
Environmental and energy use differences

All three options use LED lighting today, so the sharpest energy differences from a decade ago, when incandescent strings were still common, have narrowed. Where permanent kits still pull ahead is efficiency per hour of actual use: at roughly 0.3 W per puck, a 100 ft run of 160 pucks draws under 50 W total, similar to a couple of traditional incandescent bulbs, whether it is running warm white in July or red and green in December. Because a permanent system gets used far more hours per year than seasonal lighting confined to December, the total energy use over a year is higher in absolute terms, but the cost per hour of light delivered is comparable to or better than most seasonal LED string alternatives.
So which one is right for your home

If you only ever want lights up for a few weeks in December and do not mind the annual labour or the recurring cost of replacing strings, seasonal lighting remains a reasonable, low-commitment choice, particularly for renters or homes where a permanent installation is not practical. If you want lights that come on automatically, look clean year round, and change colour for every occasion from Christmas to Canada Day without another trip up the ladder, a permanent kit pays for itself within a few seasons compared to professional seasonal installation, and outlasts consumer adhesive strips by a wide margin. Browse kit sizes and pricing at /diy-kits or see the full product range at /shop to compare against what you are currently spending on seasonal lighting.

There is no universally correct answer here, only the one that matches how often you actually want the lights on and how many more years you want to be climbing a ladder in November and again in January.

faq.q: Is a permanent lighting kit actually cheaper than seasonal Christmas lights?
faq.a: Over several years, usually yes, particularly compared to professional seasonal installation, which runs $25 to $40 per foot per season in Canada and can exceed the entire cost of a permanent kit within one or two seasons. Compared to DIY seasonal strings, the permanent kit costs more upfront but eliminates the recurring replacement cost and labour of putting strings up and down every year.

faq.q: How does a permanent kit compare to Govee or Eufy strip lights?
faq.a: Consumer strips like Govee and Eufy cost less per foot upfront, roughly two to four dollars a foot versus a permanent kit's per-foot cost, but they are adhesive-mounted with visible wiring and typically need replacement within three to five years as the adhesive and flexible substrate degrade outdoors. A permanent kit is track-mounted, sealed to IP68, and rated for 50,000 hours with a 5-year warranty.

faq.q: Can I use a permanent system for more than just Christmas?
faq.a: Yes, that is the main advantage over seasonal lighting. The WLED controller offers 16 million colours plus a warm white channel, so the same system handles Christmas red and green, Halloween orange, Canada Day red and white, sports team colours, birthdays, and a plain warm white porch light the rest of the year.

faq.q: Do I need an electrician to install a permanent kit?
faq.a: No, for a standard residential install. The system runs on 12V, is CSA Class 2 low voltage, and the power supply and controller plug into an existing outdoor GFCI outlet, similar to plugging in seasonal LED strings. No permit or electrician is required for a typical home.

faq.q: How long do seasonal LED strings actually last outdoors?
faq.a: Most seasonal LED strings show failed sections, connector corrosion or noticeable colour fade within two to five seasons of outdoor use and storage, especially if not stored carefully between seasons. This is well short of a permanent kit's 50,000-hour puck rating and 5-year parts warranty.

faq.q: Is a permanent system worth it if I only decorate for Christmas?
faq.a: It can still make sense if you value not doing ladder work twice a year and want a cleaner, flush-mounted look rather than clipped-on strings, but the value case is strongest for homeowners who plan to use the colour-changing capability beyond December. If Christmas is genuinely the only time you want lights on, seasonal strings remain a reasonable lower-commitment option.
